info.bio: Crosby, Stills & Nash (and Young) (comúnmente conocida como CSN o CSNY) es una banda de rock and roll y folk-rock fundada en 1968. Algunos, sobre todo en Estados Unidos, la comparaban en popularidad a los Beatles. En su origen, el grupo se formó por la incorporación de Graham Nash, procedente del grupo The Hollies (Inglaterra), más David Crosby, miembro fundador de The Byrds y Stephen Stills antiguo componente de Buffalo Springfield; más tarde se incorporó Neil Young, también procedente del mismo grupo.

scenes.name: Country-rock y roots-rock
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: En los setenta, el reajuste a los viejos valores (blues, folk, country) convierte al rock en uno de los mayores éxitos del consumismo: el Establishment ya no intenta destruirlo, lo absorbe. El country-rock de Gram Parsons es una moda enorme: Commander Cody, New Riders Of The Purple Sage, Manassas, Nitty Gritty Dirt Band, Poco y los Eagles (Desperado, Hotel California); en Nashville surgen los «outlaws» (Waylon Jennings, Willie Nelson, Kris Kristofferson). El roots-rock sigue con Hot Tuna, Little Feat y Doobie Brothers, y la nostalgia recupera el blues (Roy Buchanan, Bonnie Raitt), la armonía vocal (Manhattan Transfer, Roches, McGarrigle Sisters) y los cincuenta (American Graffiti).

podcast.title: "Ohio" Single Cover Art (1970)
podcast.body: The single for "Ohio" featured a striking cover photograph of the United States Constitution riddled with four bullet holes, a direct and powerful visual commentary on the Kent State shootings. "Cover was a picture of the Constitution with four bullet holes in it."

podcast.title: Kent State Impact on CSNY's Future (1970)
podcast.body: The internal conflicts within CSNY were legendary, and the tour for their "Deja Vu" album was cut short due to these issues and technical problems at their first show in Denver on May 12, 1970, where Neil Young reportedly threw down his guitar and threatened to leave. David Crosby and Neil Young were at their road manager's house in Northern California, reassessing the band's future, when Young was inspired to write "Ohio" after seeing the Life Magazine photo. "The tour to support that record was over before it ever started. The internal conflict in CSNY is rather legendary."

podcast.title: Misinterpretation of "Ohio" in Akron (1970)
podcast.body: Johnny Andrews of WHLO in Akron, Ohio, played "Ohio" extensively, where it reached number one by mid-July. However, his interpretation was that the song was a message to protesters to "cool it for a while or get shot," which he believed was "the proper thing," completely misconstruing its anti-war and anti-violence message. "Our interpretation was that it was a rock group giving a message to protesters to cool it for a while or get shot."

podcast.title: Prioritizing "Ohio" Release (1970)
podcast.body: The president of CSNY's record company, Ahmet Ertegun (transcribed as Almitard), flew the master tape of "Ohio" on a red-eye flight from Los Angeles to New York to ensure its immediate release. This decision led to pulling "Teach Your Children," a song already climbing the charts and poised to be a number one hit, to get "Ohio" out quickly. "President of our record company, a wonderful man named Almitard, who was him Los Angeles that night when we finished recording and he took tape and flew to New York on the red eye. He said, I want this out now."

podcast.title: Stephen Stills' Initial Hesitation with "Ohio" (1970)
podcast.body: After "Ohio" was recorded, Stephen Stills expressed some reservations about the lyrics. He found it hard to believe that the National Guard would open fire with live ammunition, thinking some members might have been told they were carrying blanks. "Even Stephen Stills was not so sure about the lyrics. He thought surely there were some members of the guard who were told that they did not have live ammunition."

podcast.title: "Godfathers of Soft Rock" Influence
podcast.body: Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young are considered strong candidates for the "godfathers of soft rock" due to their significant influence on many mid-to-late 1970s bands that achieved hits with soft rock sounds, particularly those emphasizing vocal harmonies. "if there is such a thing as godfathers of soft rock I think you could make a very strong case for crossbeast is nation young so many of the bands of the mid to late 70s who had hits with the soft rock sound especially those who leaned into harmony credited CS and why with being a major influence."

podcast.title: David Crosby's Harmonic Genius
podcast.body: David Crosby, despite his "famously difficult" reputation, was a "musical genius" responsible for arranging most, if not all, of the harmonies on *Déjà Vu*. His work in this area "plants the seeds for the soft rock boom to come." "he arranged most if not all of the harmonies on this record and in doing so he plants the seeds for the soft rock boom to come."

podcast.title: Individual Success Before CSNY
podcast.body: All four members—Neil Young, David Crosby, Stephen Stills, and Graham Nash—had already achieved success in other very successful bands before forming CSNY. They were established musicians with strong opinions, not a group of beginners. "You have to keep in mind that each one of these guys, Young Crosby, Stephen Stills, Graham Nash, they had already been part of other very successful bands."

podcast.title: Influence on America and Misattribution
podcast.body: The band America was frequently compared to CSNY, or even accused of being "CSNY knockoffs." When America's song "A Horse with No Name" was released in 1971, its sound was so similar that many listeners mistakenly believed it was a Neil Young track. "And being either compared to CSNY or being accused of being CSNY knockoffs depending on your perspective in fact when horse with no name hit the airwaves and the turntables in 1971 many people thought that this was Neil Young."

concerts.title: Fillmore East (New York, Early June 1970)
concerts.body: After a soundcheck at this legendary venue, staff members approached the band to thank them for writing "Ohio," demonstrating the song's immediate impact and resonance with the public. "When the band gathered, though at the legendary Philmore East in New York in early June 1970, staff members approached them after the soundcheck and they thanked them for writing the song."
